what: Colossus Mark 1, installed at Bletchley Park, attacked its first Lorenz-cipher message (processing intercepted traffic for the Allies).

sources.title: Colossus computer
sources.quote: It was operational in January and it successfully attacked its first message on 5 February 1944.

note: Checked for earlier candidates; none found that fits the definition and kind with a verifiable source. Original note: Delivered to Bletchley 18 Jan 1944 and operational that month; first real message 5 Feb 1944. Rejected as earlier: ABC (never used for real work). ENIAC's first real program (Dec 1945) is later.

what: Bell Labs applied convolutional neural networks trained by backpropagation (LeNet) to handwritten digit recognition for zip codes, later reading cheques in ATMs.

sources.title: LeNet
sources.quote: In 1989, Yann LeCun et al. at Bell Labs first applied the backpropagation algorithm to practical applications

note: Checked for earlier candidates; none found that fits the definition and kind with a verifiable source. Original note: Widrow and Hoff's ADALINE (1960) and MADALINE (largest built 1963) adaptive filters are described by Wikipedia as 'likely the first artificial neural network applied to a real-world problem' (phone-line echo removal), which would be earlier, but I found no dated first deployment. The CIA studied the Mark I Perceptron 1960-64 only as an evaluation.

what: Google Translate switched to the neural machine translation system GNMT in November 2016, putting neural networks in daily use by very large numbers of ordinary people.

sources.title: Google Neural Machine Translation
sources.quote: In November 2016, Google Neural Machine Translation system (GNMT) was introduced.

note: Checked for earlier candidates; none found that fits the definition and kind with a verifiable source. Original note: Year is a judgment: ordinary people used neural networks unknowingly earlier (cheque reading from the 1990s, speech recognition from the early 2010s) and no source states when use became routine.

what: Leonard Adleman (USC) solved a seven-node directed Hamiltonian path problem using DNA molecules in a test tube.

sources.title: DNA computing
sources.quote: Adleman demonstrated a proof-of-concept use of DNA as a form of computation which solved the seven-point Hamiltonian path problem.

sources.title: DNA computing
sources.quote: the field originally started with the demonstration of a computing application by Leonard Adleman in 1994

note: Checked for earlier candidates; none found that fits the definition and kind with a verifiable source. Original note: No earlier computation by living cells or organic chemistry in a deliberately built computer was found; later demonstrations include DNA walkers (2003) and 3-SAT with 20 variables (2002). Publication month (Science, Nov 1994) is from the first pass, not confirmed here. No practical use or mass adoption: still laboratory research.

what: Texas Instruments' 'Cal Tech' prototype, led by Jack Kilby, was the first handheld electronic calculator (paper-tape output).

sources.title: Calculator
sources.quote: The first handheld calculator was a 1967 prototype called Cal Tech

note: Checked for earlier candidates; none found that fits the definition and kind with a verifiable source. Original note: Earlier: the Curta (1947) was a mechanical, not electronic and not battery-powered. Desktop electronic calculators from 1961 (ANITA) were too big to be pocket devices. Wikidata gives only 'start time: 1960s' for 'calculator'.

what: The first commercially produced portable electronic calculators (Sanyo ICC-0081, Canon Pocketronic, Sharp QT-8B) appeared in Japan.

sources.title: Calculator
sources.quote: The first commercially produced portable calculators appeared in Japan in 1970

note: Checked for earlier candidates; none found that fits the definition and kind with a verifiable source. Original note: Earlier than the first pass (Bowmar 1971, HP-35 1972). Sharp EL-8 (Jan 1971) was close to pocket size. Exact 1970 month not given.

what: Pocket electronic calculators became popular as integrated circuits cut their size and cost.

sources.title: Calculator
sources.quote: They became popular in the mid-1970s as the incorporation of integrated circuits reduced their size and cost.

note: Checked for earlier candidates; none found that fits the definition and kind with a verifiable source. Original note: 'Mid-1970s' is the source's wording; 1975 is my choice of year.

what: Psion launched the Organiser, a pocket computer with a one-line LCD and database; Wikipedia calls it the 'world's first practical pocket computer'.

sources.title: Psion Organiser
sources.quote: Launched in 1984,  the Psion Organiser was the "world's first practical pocket computer".

note: Checked for earlier candidates; none found that fits the definition and kind with a verifiable source. Original note: Same event as first_practical_use. Earlier candidates: Pitroda's 1975 electronic diary patent (no device found); Sharp PC-1211 pocket computer (March 1980, a programmable computer, not a notes/schedule device); Thorp and Shannon's 1961 shoe roulette computer (not a notes device). Organiser II (1986) is the first 'usable' PDA per Wikipedia.

what: Psion Organiser sold in the UK as a pocket diary and database computer.

sources.title: Personal digital assistant
sources.quote: The first PDA, the Organiser, was released in 1984 by Psion

note: Checked for earlier candidates; none found that fits the definition and kind with a verifiable source. Original note: Same date as demonstration; the Organiser I was a commercial product from the start.

what: Palm's PalmPilot handhelds (first Palm line March 1996, PalmPilot March 1997) reportedly sold over a million units by 1998.

sources.title: PalmPilot
sources.quote: PalmPilot had reportedly sold over 1 million units by 1998.

note: Checked for earlier candidates; none found that fits the definition and kind with a verifiable source. Original note: The page gives a sales figure rather than a 'became common' date, so 1998 is a judgment; Apple Newton (1993) sold poorly.

what: Robot Scientist 'Adam' (Aberystwyth/Cambridge, Ross King) autonomously generated and tested hypotheses on yeast genes and found new knowledge

sources.title: Robot Scientist
sources.quote: Adam became the first machine in history to have discovered new scientific knowledge independently of its human creators.

note: Checked for earlier candidates; none found that fits the definition and kind with a verifiable source. Original note: Year 2009 (Science, 2 April 2009) is from memory/first pass: the pages I could reach (Wikipedia only) give no year. Earlier candidates: DENDRAL (1960s, Stanford; Wikipedia says it aimed to study hypothesis formation and discovery in science) and Meta-DENDRAL (mid-1970s, proposed new mass-spectrometry rules) are partial fits (analysis and rule induction but no experiments, human-directed) and I could not source dates. So earlier event may exist. Possible earlier: the 2004 Nature paper by King et al. (first Robot Scientist closed-loop hypothesis and experiment on yeast), but no fetchable page gave a quotable source, so 2009 kept.

what: Lockheed's interactive Dialog system (Roger Summit) was tested on NASA's STAR database at Ames in 1966, cutting searches from 14 hours to a few minutes; this became NASA RECON.

sources.title: Roger K. Summit
sources.quote: Information searches within the NASA STAR database went from taking 14 hours, plus shipping and handling, to a few minutes with Summit's Dialog system.

sources.title: Dialog (online database)
sources.quote: The earliest form of the Dialog system was completed in 1966 in Lockheed under the direction of Roger K. Summit.

note: Replaces MEDLINE late 1971: Dialog was online and interactive on a large NASA database in 1966 (Ames experiment, NASA contract 1966). Result time is 'a few minutes' not strictly seconds, and 1966 was an experiment before RECON (1967 award); MEDLARS 1964 was batch. Original note: Rejected earlier: MEDLARS 1964 (launched by NLM, 'first large-scale, computer-based, retrospective search service available to the general public') was a real service but batch-mode, so it does not meet 'in seconds'. Dialog commercial service started ~1972 (not sourced). If batch counts, practical use is 1964.
